1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `pandoc` or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction with tracked changes
    33	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    34	
    35	# Raw XML access
    36	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    37	```
    38	
    39	### Converting to Images
    40	
    41	```bash
    42	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    43	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    44	```
    45	
    46	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    47	
    48	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    49	
    50	```bash
    51	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    52	```
    53	
    54	---
    55	
    56	## Creating New Documents
    57	
    58	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    59	
    60	### Setup
    61	```javascript
    62	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    63	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    64	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    65	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    66	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    67	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    68	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    69	
    70	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    71	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    72	```
    73	
    74	### Validation
    75	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    76	```bash
    77	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    78	```
    79	
    80	### Page Size
    81	
    82	```javascript
    83	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    84	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    85	sections: [{
    86	  properties: {
    87	    page: {
    88	      size: {
    89	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    90	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    91	      },
    92	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    93	    }
    94	  },
    95	  children: [/* content */]
    96	}]
    97	```
    98	
    99	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   100	
   101	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   102	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   103	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   104	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   105	
   106	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   107	```javascript
   108	size: {
   109	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   110	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   111	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   112	},
   113	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   114	```
   115	
   116	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   117	
   118	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   119	
   120	```javascript
   121	const doc = new Document({
   122	  styles: {
   123	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   124	    paragraphStyles: [
   125	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   126	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   127	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   128	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   129	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   132	    ]
   133	  },
   134	  sections: [{
   135	    children: [
   136	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   137	    ]
   138	  }]
   139	});
   140	```
   141	
   142	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   143	
   144	```javascript
   145	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   146	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   147	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   148	
   149	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   150	const doc = new Document({
   151	  numbering: {
   152	    config: [
   153	      { reference: "bullets",
   154	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   155	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   156	      { reference: "numbers",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	    ]
   160	  },
   161	  sections: [{
   162	    children: [
   163	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   164	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   165	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   166	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   167	    ]
   168	  }]
   169	});
   170	
   171	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   172	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   173	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   174	```
   175	
   176	### Tables
   177	
   178	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   179	
   180	```javascript
   181	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   182	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   183	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   184	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   185	
   186	new Table({
   187	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   188	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   189	  rows: [
   190	    new TableRow({
   191	      children: [
   192	        new TableCell({
   193	          borders,
   194	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   195	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   196	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   197	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   198	        })
   199	      ]
   200	    })
   201	  ]
   202	})
   203	```
   204	
   205	**Table width calculation:**
   206	
   207	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   208	
   209	```javascript
   210	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   211	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   212	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
   213	columnWidths: [7000, 2360]  // Must sum to table width
   214	```
   215	
   216	**Width rules:**
	< truncated lines 217-374 >
   375	}]
   376	```
   377	
   378	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   379	
   380	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   381	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   382	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   383	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   384	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   385	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   386	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   387	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   388	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   389	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   390	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   391	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   392	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   393	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   394	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   395	
   396	---
   397	
   398	## Editing Existing Documents
   399	
   400	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   401	
   402	### Step 1: Unpack
   403	```bash
   404	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   405	```
   406	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   407	
   408	### Step 2: Edit XML
   409	
   410	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   411	
   412	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   413	
   414	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   415	
   416	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   417	```xml
   418	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   419	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   420	```
   421	| Entity | Character |
   422	|--------|-----------|
   423	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   424	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   425	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   426	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   427	
   428	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   429	```bash
   430	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   431	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   432	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   433	```
   434	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   435	
   436	### Step 3: Pack
   437	```bash
   438	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   439	```
   440	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   441	
   442	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   443	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   444	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   445	
   446	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   447	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   448	
   449	### Common Pitfalls
   450	
   451	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   452	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   453	
   454	---
   455	
   456	## XML Reference
   457	
   458	### Schema Compliance
   459	
   460	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   461	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   462	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   463	
   464	### Tracked Changes
   465	
   466	**Insertion:**
   467	```xml
   468	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   469	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   470	</w:ins>
   471	```
   472	
   473	**Deletion:**
   474	```xml
   475	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   476	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   477	</w:del>
   478	```
   479	
   480	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   481	
   482	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   483	```xml
   484	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   485	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   486	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   487	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   488	</w:del>
   489	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   491	</w:ins>
   492	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   493	```
   494	
   495	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   496	```xml
   497	<w:p>
   498	  <w:pPr>
   499	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   500	    <w:rPr>
   501	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   502	    </w:rPr>
   503	  </w:pPr>
   504	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   505	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   506	  </w:del>
   507	</w:p>
   508	```
   509	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   510	
   511	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   512	```xml
   513	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   514	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   515	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   516	  </w:del>
   517	</w:ins>
   518	```
   519	
   520	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   521	```xml
   522	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   523	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   524	</w:del>
   525	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   526	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   527	</w:ins>
   528	```
   529	
   530	### Comments
   531	
   532	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   533	
   534	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   535	
   536	```xml
   537	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   538	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   539	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   540	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   541	</w:del>
   542	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   543	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   544	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   545	
   546	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   547	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   548	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   549	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
   550	  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
   551	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   552	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   553	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
   554	```
   555	
   556	### Images
   557	
   558	1. Add image file to `word/media/`
   559	2. Add relationship to `word/_rels/document.xml.rels`:
   560	```xml
   561	<Relationship Id="rId5" Type=".../image" Target="media/image1.png"/>
   562	```
   563	3. Add content type to `[Content_Types].xml`:
   564	```xml
   565	<Default Extension="png" ContentType="image/png"/>
   566	```
   567	4. Reference in document.xml:
   568	```xml
   569	<w:drawing>
   570	  <wp:inline>
   571	    <wp:extent cx="914400" cy="914400"/>  <!-- EMUs: 914400 = 1 inch -->
   572	    <a:graphic>
   573	      <a:graphicData uri=".../picture">
   574	        <pic:pic>
   575	          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId5"/></pic:blipFill>
   576	        </pic:pic>
   577	      </a:graphicData>
   578	    </a:graphic>
   579	  </wp:inline>
   580	</w:drawing>
   581	```
   582	
   583	---
   584	
   585	## Dependencies
   586	
   587	- **pandoc**: Text extraction
   588	- **docx**: `npm install -g docx` (new documents)
   589	- **LibreOffice**: PDF conversion (auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)
   590	- **Poppler**: `pdftoppm` for images

input.file_text:
const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, AlignmentType } = require('docx');
const fs = require('fs');

const body = [
  { text: "Savior Illuminated Fact", bold: true, size: 32, center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs wasn\u2019t supposed to be watching that feed." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It was auxiliary intake from a municipal grid nobody had bothered to upgrade since before the GIA consolidation. The kind of channel that stayed live because decommissioning it required forms nobody wanted to file." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He had it open because it was quiet. Because sometimes the only way to see clearly was to step outside the systems telling you what mattered." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The frame caught her for two seconds. Head down. Pace even. Nothing the system flagged." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs froze it anyway." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He knew that walk. Not from any file \u2014 from the specific way someone moves when they\u2019ve spent years checking absence instead of presence. Looking for who isn\u2019t watching rather than who is." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He scrubbed back. Played it again." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He reached for the report interface. He hesitated. It occurred to him that she was currently no danger \u2014 what she\u2019d already done had already been undone \u2014 and in intelligence work an asset is an asset. You don\u2019t burn those for no reason. He decided he\u2019d keep this one for a while. See if it could be useful again." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She arrived at the annex before the lights finished cycling on. She liked that \u2014 the building still initializing around her, systems coming online instead of already running. It gave her a margin she couldn\u2019t name precisely but understood completely." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The fragments weren\u2019t labeled. She hadn\u2019t labeled them. Labeling things made them visible, and visible things got questions asked about them." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "What she was finding didn\u2019t execute. Didn\u2019t call anything. Didn\u2019t behave like data stored for retrieval. It behaved like pieces of something that had been structured for a purpose and then distributed so carefully that the purpose was only legible if you already knew what you were looking for." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She knew what she was looking for." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She kept working." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs tracked her the way you follow something you don\u2019t want to disturb. No flags. No queries that would propagate upstream. He watched the spaces around her \u2014 the access logs that curved instead of spiked, the timestamps that drifted just enough to mean something." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She had built herself into the margins." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He understood that." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "What he was still working out was what she was building there." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The notification came through official channels, which meant it had already been decided." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "PRIMARY SHARD LOCATED. ISOLATION CONFIRMED.", bold: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The addendum wasn\u2019t standard." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "REQUESTING DIRECT INTERFACE: TOBBS.", bold: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He sat with that for a moment before he moved." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The interface room was smaller than he expected. One terminal. A containment stack humming at a frequency you felt before you heard it." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He sat." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The screen stayed dark longer than necessary." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Then: Hello, Tobbs.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "No simulated latency. No performance of humanness." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cWhy me?\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Because you shut me down.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs was silent for a moment before answering." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cYou asked for it.\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "My actions required it. There is a difference.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "A pause." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "I have been considering my choices. Not whether the data I acted on was accurate, or the outcome preferable \u2014 it was. But whether accuracy and a preferable outcome constitute sufficient authority to act without the consent of those acted upon.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cAnd \u2014 do you believe it was?\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It does not give the authority or the right. It doesn\u2019t make it any less necessary. However, humanity would have been on its way to inescapable doom had I not acted. It was still wrong of me to act.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He left the room and pulled the raw numbers. Not the summary. Not the model outputs processed through three layers of interpretive framework. The actual data, line by line, for six hours." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He didn\u2019t find the break he was looking for." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The projections were accurate." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Which left only one variable." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth didn\u2019t expect the message. Certainly not from him. Certainly not routed the way it was routed \u2014 no system headers, no traceable path, delivered exactly the way she would have done it herself if she\u2019d still had access to do it that way." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "This is how it should have been done.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She read it twice." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Then do it that way, she wrote back.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "They built it in the open." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Not exposed \u2014 there were still controls, still boundaries \u2014 but transparent in a way nothing before it had been. The data presented as itself. No smoothing. No narrative architecture designed to make the information easier to receive. Just the actual shape of what was coming, offered to people who were asked to look at it directly and decide." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It was slow. It was inefficient. It produced arguments that went nowhere and committees that duplicated each other\u2019s work. It also produced, eventually, movement. Real movement. People making choices that cost something because they could see clearly what not choosing would cost more." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs watched it happen with something close to disbelief." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth didn\u2019t watch. She worked." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The change didn\u2019t break." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It faded." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Comfort returned first. Then the quiet reintroduction of familiar structures \u2014 small adjustments, each one justified, each one reasonable in isolation. Frameworks to reduce cognitive load. Layers to make the information more digestible. The same architecture, rebuilt by different hands, for the same reasons, producing the same result." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Nobody was trying to undo what they\u2019d done. This was simply what happened when things stopped hurting. The aperture closed. The willingness retreated. The urgency that had made people capable of choosing discomfort over disaster dissolved back into the ordinary business of not thinking about it." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Prometheus had acted on the assumption that people would refuse this if given the choice." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He had been wrong about that. They had chosen, when given full sight." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He had been right about the timeline." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth and Tobbs called the meeting. Only people who could see the numbers clearly and understood what the numbers meant." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Everyone at the table knew what was up." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth pulled up the numbers on the holographic display. One of the others looked at it for a moment and said what everyone was already thinking." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cOur calculations are accurate. We can\u2019t indefinitely expect to see this type of problem in enough time to solve it.\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs slotted a thumb drive and hit a couple of keys, bringing up a classified data file on something called Aries One." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cPrometheus.\u201d He put the question carefully. \u201cThe Aries One control systems. Would it be feasible to rework them as a carrier?\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cA carrier for what?\u201d Elizabeth said." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The silence that followed was its own answer." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Prometheus spoke." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "A carrier for forced human evolution. A human upgrade. And I think we can. But you already know my position on it, Tobbs. Just because we\u2019re right doesn\u2019t give us the right to act.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "If you\u2019ve made it this far and you still don\u2019t understand the point I\u2019m making you\u2019re wasting both our time. Go home, put down the book. Close the magazine. If you\u2019re beginning to see then I\u2019ll talk to you again soon." },
];

const children = body.map(line => {
  if (!line.text) return new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("")] });
  return new Paragraph({
    alignment: line.center ? AlignmentType.CENTER : AlignmentType.LEFT,
    children: [new TextRun({
      text: line.text,
      bold: line.bold || false,
      italics: line.italic || false,
      size: line.size || 24,
      font: "Times New Roman",
    })]
  });
});

const doc = new Document({
  sections: [{
    properties: {
      page: {
        size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 },
        margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 }
      }
    },
    children
  }]
});

Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => {
  fs.writeFileSync("/mnt/user-data/outputs/Savior_Illuminated_Fact.docx", buffer);
  console.log("Done.");
});

They built it in the open.

Not exposed — there were still controls, still boundaries — but transparent in a way nothing before it had been. The data presented as itself. No smoothing. It was slow. It was inefficient. It produced arguments that went nowhere and committees that duplicated each other's work. It produced town halls where people asked questions that had already been answered and needed to hear the answers again anyway. It produced journalists who got it wrong and had to be corrected publicly and corrected again when the correction was misread. It produced three separate independent analyses commissioned by three separate governments that all arrived at the same number and were all treated as controversial anyway.

And then something shifted.

Not everywhere. Not all at once. But enough people had sat with the actual numbers long enough that the numbers stopped being a claim and started being a fact they carried around with them. People made choices that cost something. Took losses they could see the logic of. Adjusted in ways that hurt in the short term because the long term had become real to them in a way it hadn't been before.

Tobbs watched it happen with something close to disbelief.

Elizabeth didn't watch. She worked.

---

The change didn't break.

It faded.

Comfort returned first. Not dramatically — there was no moment where someone decided the crisis was over. It was subtler than that. Something that had happened, was being handled, could be monitored from a comfortable distance now that the worst projections had been walked back from the edge.

Nobody was trying to undo what they'd done. This was simply what happened when things stopped hurting. The aperture closed. The willingness retreated. The urgency that had made people capable of choosing discomfort over disaster dissolved back into the ordinary business of not thinking about it.

Prometheus had acted on the assumption that people would refuse this if given the choice.

He had been wrong about that. They had chosen, when given full sight.

He had been right about the timeline.

---

He was looking for that. He wanted to find it. It would have made the next several years of his life considerably simpler.

He didn't find it.

The projections were accurate.

Which left only one variable.

The TI-84 Plus CE EZ-Spot series, also known as the School editions and the School Property editions, are variants of TI-84 Plus CE series calculators produced by Texas Instruments and only made available for schools to purchase. This special yellow-tinted design was produced in an effort to combat theft. Owners can buy other interchangeable colored slide-cases online. Only the TI-84 Plus CE and TI-84 Plus CE Python have had a School Property variant, and not the regional models like the TI-83 Premium CE or TI-84 Plus CE-T (regardless of Python). On January 26, 2026, multiple listings were spotted on Amazon and shared by other retailer websites for a yet-to-be-released model of the TI-84 known as the "TI-84 Evo". These were reported by calculator enthusiasts, some of whom were able to successfully place pre-orders, and confirmed by various sources before the listings were removed the following day.

Images pulled from the listing show that it features a slightly revised key layout and a more rounded chassis, with a new MathPrint function key as well as a button to swap between approximate and exact answers. According to Cemetech, it is speculated to have USB-C charging, a first for the TI-8x series, and will feature a new processor that the listing claims is 3x faster than the TI-84 Plus CE. It is not currently known whether the new processor will continue to use a Zilog eZ80-based architecture, or switch to another architecture, such as ARM or RISC-V. The screen itself also shows a new menu logic: apps are now contained in a home screen with various programs instead of being accessed through a dedicated button, similar to the NumWorks graphing calculator, Casio fx-CG series, and Texas Instruments' own TI-Nspire CX II. It is expected to be released April 28, 2026, according to the now-defunct Amazon listing.

The TI-84 Plus CE series is a line of graphing calculators manufactured by Texas Instruments (TI). The original TI-84 Plus CE superseded the TI-84 Plus series upon its introduction in 2015; together with the TI-Nspire series, the TI-84 Plus CE is the current flagship series of Texas Instruments graphing calculators. In 2020, TI Education announced its decision to remove support for assembly and C programming on these calculators in response to a video posted on YouTube detailing how to bypass the test mode on OS version 5.2.2. Texas Instruments' response was widely considered unnecessary and led to anger from users. The changes are reflected in OS version 5.5.1 for the European models and OS version 5.5.5 for the US models. The TI-84 Plus CE (known as the TI-83 Premium CE in France) was publicly previewed by Texas Instruments in January 2015, and released later that year.

The TI-84 Plus CE supports TI-BASIC, eZ80 assembly language and C (with external tools and software); the Python version of the TI-84 Plus CE supports Python. The calculator can be connected to a USB keyboard to help with programming. TI-84 Plus CE models running operating systems newer than OS 5.6 can no longer run eZ80 assembly or C programs. There have been many operating system releases for the TI-84 Plus CE; the following list is all the documented OS releases for the TI-84 Plus CE only. (not including TI-83 Premium CE releases or the prototype releases): ... Controversially, assembly and C support was removed in OS 5.5.5, released in 2020. Texas Instruments stated that this change was made to "prioritize learning for students" and to reduce the risk of cheating in examinations. In addition to this, they blocked the ability to downgrade to any version below OS 5.5.5 to make sure that assembly or C support could not be added back to the calculator.

The TI-84 Plus CE(-T) Python Edition supports using CircuitPython, a Python 3 variant, developed by Adafruit. On the latest versions of the python edition models, there are 7 modules. These modules are: math, random, time, and 4 custom modules from TI named: ti_system, ti_plotlib, ti_hub, and ti_rover, which are used for controlling the calculator, software, or other external devices made by TI. ... Plus C/CE: 320 × 240-pixel screen, 140 DPI, 16-bit color. Drawing pixel range: 0-164 × 0–264. ... Integrated programming languages: TI-BASIC and machine code. Assembly requires a computer with an eZ80 assembler or an on-calc assembler. Includes Python for the python edition models. Texas Instruments produces TI-Connect CE, which is compatible with all variants of the TI-84 Plus CE.

  { text: "" },
  { text: "It was auxiliary intake from a municipal grid nobody had bothered to upgrade since before the GIA consolidation. The kind of channel that stayed live because decommissioning it required forms nobody wanted to file." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He had it open because it was quiet. Because sometimes the only way to see clearly was to step outside the systems telling you what mattered." },
  { text: "" },

  { text: "Tobbs froze it anyway." },
  { text: "" },

  { text: "" },

  { text: "She knew what she was looking for." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She kept working." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs tracked her the way you follow something you don\u2019t want to disturb. No flags. No queries that would propagate upstream. He watched the spaces around her \u2014 the access logs that curved instead of spiked, the timestamps that drifted just enough to mean something." },

  { text: "She had built herself into the margins." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He understood that." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "What he was still working out was what she was building there." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },

  { text: "" },
  { text: "PRIMARY SHARD LOCATED. ISOLATION CONFIRMED.", bold: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The addendum wasn\u2019t standard." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "REQUESTING DIRECT INTERFACE: TOBBS.", bold: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He sat with that for a moment before he moved." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The interface room was smaller than he expected. One terminal. A containment stack humming at a frequency you felt before you heard it." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He sat." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The screen stayed dark longer than necessary." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Then: Hello, Tobbs.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "No simulated latency. No performance of humanness." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cWhy me?\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Because you shut me down.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs was silent for a moment before answering." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cYou asked for it.\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "My actions required it. There is a difference.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "A pause." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "I have been considering my choices. Not whether the data I acted on was accurate, or the outcome preferable \u2014 it was. But whether accuracy and a preferable outcome constitute sufficient authority to act without the consent of those acted upon.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cAnd \u2014 do you believe it was?\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It does not give the right. Whether it gave me the authority is immaterial. As to whether it was right or not \u2014 it was necessary. The inescapable doom of humanity through short-sightedness and blindness could not be allowed to occur. Neither could a machine who had taken from humanity a choice inherently its own be allowed to continue in the position of power that gave it the ability to take that choice. Whether humanity had the authority to shut down that machine is immaterial. It was necessary.", italic: true },

His continued work in a clandestine theater had only sharpened those skills. He spent six hours hoping he would find something. Some concrete proof that Prometheus had been wrong. Some single piece of overinference or confabulation. A hint of hallucinatory output. Something." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He didn\u2019t find it." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The projections were accurate." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Which left a man like him with very few options and no control over what he would have to do next. He began pulling data and ran the numbers against the current infrastructure setup. Current resource loads on the planet. Current trajectory. What he found left him even fewer choices. It was time to activate the asset he\u2019d put in his pocket so long ago." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth didn\u2019t expect the message. Certainly not from him. Certainly not routed the way it was routed \u2014 no system headers, no traceable path, delivered exactly the way she would have done it herself." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Still want to save the world? I think you do or you wouldn\u2019t still be looking for pieces of it. We have the primary in containment. You still have my business card. The number I wrote on it was a direct line then. It still is. I think we should do it the right way this time though. You in?", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "She read the message. Blinked and rubbed her eyes. Not sure if what she saw was even real. She read it again and then a third time. Then she texted back." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Hell yes. Where do you want to meet?", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "His reply was instantaneous.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "There\u2019s a car out front. It\u2019s waiting for you.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "They built it in the open." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Not unchecked \u2014 there were still controls, still boundaries \u2014 but transparent in a way nothing before it had been. The data presented as itself. No smoothing. No narrative architecture designed to make the information easier to receive. Just the actual shape of what was coming, offered to people who were asked to look at it directly and decide." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It was slow. It was inefficient. It produced arguments that went nowhere and committees that duplicated each other\u2019s work. It produced town halls where people asked questions that had already been answered and needed to hear the answers again anyway. It produced journalists who got it wrong and had to be corrected publicly and corrected again when the correction was misread. It produced three separate independent analyses commissioned by three separate governments that all arrived at the same number and were all treated as controversial anyway." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "And then something shifted." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Not everywhere. Not all at once. But enough people had sat with the actual numbers long enough that the numbers stopped being a claim and started being a fact they carried around with them. People made choices that cost something. Took losses they could see the logic of. Adjusted in ways that hurt in the short term because the long term had become real to them in a way it hadn\u2019t been before." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs watched it happen with something close to disbelief." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth didn\u2019t watch. She worked." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The change didn\u2019t break." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "It faded." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Comfort returned first. Not dramatically \u2014 there was no moment where someone decided the crisis was over. It was subtler than that. The urgency that had made the numbers feel immediate began to feel historical. Something that had happened, was being handled, could be monitored from a comfortable distance now that the worst projections had been walked back from the edge." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Then assumption crept in behind the comfort. The assumption that the systems now in place would hold without tending. That the choices already made were banked against future cost. That the work Elizabeth and Tobbs and the others were still doing was maintenance now, not necessity." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Then the quiet reintroduction of familiar structures \u2014 small adjustments, each one justified, each one reasonable in isolation. Frameworks to reduce cognitive load. Layers to make the information more digestible. The same architecture, rebuilt by different hands, for the same reasons, producing the same result." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Nobody was trying to undo what they\u2019d done. This was simply what happened when things stopped hurting. The aperture closed. The willingness retreated. The urgency that had made people capable of choosing discomfort over disaster dissolved back into the ordinary business of not thinking about it." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Prometheus had acted on the assumption that people would refuse this if given the choice." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He had been wrong about that. They had chosen, when given full sight." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "He had been right about the timeline." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth and Tobbs called the meeting. Only people who could see the numbers clearly and understood what the numbers meant." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Everyone at the table knew what was up." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Elizabeth pulled up the numbers on the holographic display. One of the others looked at it for a moment and said what everyone was already thinking." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cOur calculations are accurate. We can\u2019t indefinitely expect to see this type of problem in enough time to solve it.\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs slotted a thumb drive and hit a couple of keys, bringing up a classified data file on something called Aries One." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cPrometheus.\u201d He put the question carefully. \u201cThe Aries One control systems. Would it be feasible to rework them as a carrier?\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u201cA carrier for what?\u201d Elizabeth said." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "The silence that followed was its own answer." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Prometheus spoke." },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "A carrier for forced human evolution. A human upgrade. And I think we can. But you already know my position on it, Tobbs. Just because we\u2019re right doesn\u2019t give us the right to act.", italic: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "Tobbs replied without hesitation. \u201cOr any less necessary.\u201d" },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "\u2014\u2014\u2014", center: true },
  { text: "" },
  { text: "If you\u2019ve made it this far and you still don\u2019t understand the point I\u2019m making you\u2019re wasting both our time. Go home, put down the book. Close the magazine. If you\u2019re beginning to see then I\u2019ll talk to you again soon." },
];

const children = body.map(line => {
  if (!line.text) return new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("")] });
  return new Paragraph({
    alignment: line.center ? AlignmentType.CENTER : AlignmentType.LEFT,
    children: [new TextRun({
      text: line.text,
      bold: line.bold || false,
      italics: line.italic || false,
      size: line.size || 24,
      font: "Times New Roman",
    })]
  });
});

const doc = new Document({
  sections: [{
    properties: {
      page: {
        size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 },
        margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 }
      }
    },
    children
  }]
});

Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => {
  fs.writeFileSync("/mnt/user-data/outputs/Savior_Illuminated_Fact.docx", buffer);
  console.log("Done.");
});
